Actus reus: the voluntary act requirement and its exclusions
Omission liability and the sources of a legal duty to act
The constitutional bar on punishing status alone (Robinson) and its limit (Powell)
Mens rea through the Model Penal Code's four culpable mental states, with the Code's non-binding status and uneven adoption
Element-by-element assignment of culpability, and surviving common-law terms (malice, specific and general intent)
Concurrence of act and mental state
Causation in result crimes: factual (but-for) and legal (proximate), including intervening superseding causes
Attendant circumstances and the result element
Strict liability offenses and the arguments for and against them

claims.claim: In U.S. criminal law an offense is defined by statute and decomposes into elements, and the Due Process Clause protects the accused against conviction except upon proof beyond a reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime charged (In re Winship, 397 U.S. 358 (1970), decided March 31, 1970).

Winship arose from a New York Family Court delinquency adjudication of a twelve-year-old decided on a preponderance standard, and the Court held the reasonable-doubt requirement applies at the adjudicatory stage of juvenile proceedings.

States codify the Winship standard: California Penal Code section 1096 provides that the effect of the presumption of innocence is to place on the state the burden of proving guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, and defines reasonable doubt in terms of jurors' inability to say they feel an abiding conviction of the truth of the charge.

The act element (actus reus) requires a voluntary bodily movement; reflexes, convulsions, movements during unconsciousness or sleep, and conduct under hypnosis are the standard examples of movements that are not voluntary acts (Model Penal Code section 2.01(2)). Thoughts alone cannot be criminalized, and one voluntary act in a course of conduct suffices even if a later movement is involuntary.

Robinson v. California, 370 U.S. 660 (1962) (argued April 17, 1962; decided June 25, 1962) held that a California statute making it a misdemeanor to 'be addicted to the use of narcotics', construed by the state courts as criminalizing the status of addiction prosecutable at any time before the offender reforms, inflicts cruel and unusual punishment in violation of the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments. Justice Frankfurter took no part; Justices Clark and White dissented.

Powell v. Texas, 392 U.S. 514 (1968) (decided June 17, 1968) affirmed a conviction for being intoxicated in a public place on the ground that the defendant was convicted not for being a chronic alcoholic but for being in public while drunk on a particular occasion, and so was not punished for a mere status; no opinion commanded a majority.

An omission satisfies the act element only where the law imposes a duty to act, and the duty then becomes an element the prosecution must prove. Courses group the recognized duties as statute, contract, status relationship, voluntary assumption of care, and creation of the peril; most U.S. jurisdictions impose no general duty to rescue a stranger.

Verified statutory examples of duties whose breach is punished as an omission: 26 U.S.C. 7203 (willful failure to file a required return, keep records, or supply information; misdemeanor, up to one year and a fine up to $25,000, or $100,000 for a corporation) and California Penal Code section 270 (parent who willfully omits without lawful excuse to furnish necessary food, clothing, shelter, or medical attendance for a minor child; misdemeanor).

The Model Penal Code's four culpable mental states, in descending order of culpability, are purpose, knowledge, recklessness, and negligence (section 2.02(2)(a)-(d)): purposely means causing the result is the actor's conscious object; knowingly means awareness the result is practically certain; recklessly means consciously disregarding a substantial and unjustifiable risk in gross deviation from accepted standards; negligently means failing to perceive such a risk one should be aware of.

The Model Penal Code is an American Law Institute model rather than binding law: precepts suggested by the Institute, like common-law principles, must bow to legislative mandates (United States v. Bailey, 444 U.S. 394 (1980)). Adoption has been uneven and older common-law vocabulary persists; Bailey described the general-intent / specific-intent distinction as a source of considerable confusion, quoting four incompatible uses of those terms.

Culpability is assigned element by element: the kind of culpability required must be faced separately with respect to each material element of the crime, as Bailey adopted from the Institute and as United States v. Feola, 420 U.S. 671 (1975), illustrated (intent to assault required, knowledge of the victim's federal status not).

Concurrence requires that the criminal act and the culpable mental state exist at the same moment, with the mental state actuating the act. California Penal Code section 20 (enacted 1872) states that in every crime or public offense there must exist a union, or joint operation, of act and intent, or criminal negligence.

Causation in result crimes is a hybrid of actual cause and legal (proximate) cause. Actual cause is ordinarily but-for cause — the Model Penal Code section 2.03(1)(a) formulation that conduct is the cause of a result if it is an antecedent but for which the result would not have occurred — which Burrage v. United States, 571 U.S. 204 (2014), called the minimum requirement for a finding of causation. Conduct that combines with other factors is still a but-for cause where those factors alone would not have produced the result.

Burrage held that, at least where the drug distributed is not an independently sufficient cause of death or serious bodily injury, a defendant is not liable under the Controlled Substances Act's death-results enhancement unless the use was a but-for cause, and that the enhancement is an element that must be submitted to the jury.

Legal or proximate causation is tested in the case law by objective foreseeability, and the Model Penal Code section 2.03(2)(b) asks whether the actual result is too remote or accidental to have a just bearing on liability; an intervening superseding cause, classically a third party's deliberate crime, cuts a defendant off from liability for the result while leaving the lesser offense actually committed.

Attendant circumstances are specified facts that must be present when the offense is committed, and a result element appears only in offenses that require a bad result; not every crime has one (attempt offenses, for example, do not).

Strict liability offenses attach no mental state to at least one element. Courts do not infer them lightly: Morissette v. United States, 342 U.S. 246 (1952), held criminal intent is an element of 18 U.S.C. 641 and that mere omission of any mention of intent does not eliminate it, and Staples v. United States, 511 U.S. 600 (1994), required proof that the defendant knew of the characteristics bringing his rifle within the machinegun definition.

The severity of the authorized penalty bears on whether a statute is read as strict liability: the public welfare offense cases almost uniformly involved light penalties such as fines or short jail terms, and the up-to-ten-year exposure in Staples confirmed the Court's refusal to dispense with mens rea. The Model Penal Code confines strict liability to offenses it calls violations, punishable by fine, forfeiture, or other civil penalty rather than imprisonment (section 2.05(1)(a)).

Strict liability is contested: critics argue it detaches liability from fault and from deterrence, since an actor who could not have known cannot be deterred, while defenders argue some public health and safety regulation is unadministrable if knowledge must be proved in every case. This is presented as a live disagreement, with the Model Penal Code's confinement of strict liability to non-imprisonable violations as one institutional response.

Element definitions vary by jurisdiction: criminal law in the United States is primarily state law, the charging statute controls, and the state and federal examples used here (California, federal tax and firearms statutes) are illustrations rather than statements of any other jurisdiction's law.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How far Robinson v. California reaches — status alone, or conduct that is a symptom of a condition
positions: Robinson bars punishing a condition such as narcotic addiction as a criminal offense
Powell v. Texas affirmed a public-intoxication conviction for a chronic alcoholic because the statute punished conduct on a particular occasion, and produced no majority opinion
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both are stated. The lesson teaches Robinson's holding as the constitutional floor under the act requirement and Powell as the limiting case, and says explicitly that no opinion in Powell commanded a majority and that courts have read Robinson narrowly.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the Model Penal Code's four mental states describe American law
positions: Courses and the Supreme Court routinely use purpose, knowledge, recklessness, and negligence as the organizing framework
The Code binds no one; states adopted it unevenly and many statutes retain malice aforethought, specific intent, and general intent
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Taught as the framework with the caveat attached in the same subsection, sourced to Bailey's statement that the Institute's precepts must bow to legislative mandates and to Bailey's account of the confusion in the older vocabulary.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether strict liability offenses are defensible
positions: They detach criminal liability from fault and cannot deter an actor who could not have known
They are administratively necessary in some public health and safety regulation
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as a live normative disagreement with both positions attributed, plus the doctrinal facts: courts require a clear signal before reading a statute as strict liability, penalty severity counts against it, and the Model Penal Code limits strict liability to non-imprisonable violations.

sourceRecords.title: Robinson v. California, 370 U.S. 660 (1962)
sourceRecords.provider: Library of Congress (United States Reports, volume 370)
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion of the United States; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read the bound U.S. Reports scan directly (host blocked the fetcher; retrieved with curl and a browser user-agent). Verified: argued April 17, 1962, decided June 25, 1962; California Health and Safety Code section 11721 made it a misdemeanor to 'be addicted to the use of narcotics'; state courts construed it as making the status of addiction criminal, prosecutable 'at any time before he reforms', without use, possession, or antisocial behavior in the state; held that as construed the statute inflicts cruel and unusual punishment in violation of the Eighth and Fourteenth Amendments; the Court's comparison to criminalizing mental illness or disease and the line that even one day in prison would be cruel and unusual for the 'crime' of having a common cold; Justice Frankfurter took no part; Justices Clark and White dissented.

sourceRecords.title: Powell v. Texas, 392 U.S. 514 (1968)
sourceRecords.provider: Library of Congress (United States Reports, volume 392)
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion of the United States; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read the bound U.S. Reports scan directly. Verified: argued March 7, 1968, decided June 17, 1968; conviction under Texas Penal Code article 477 for being found intoxicated in a public place was affirmed; the syllabus and Justice Marshall's opinion for four Justices state that appellant was convicted 'not for being a chronic alcoholic, but for being in public while drunk on a particular occasion' and so was not punished for a mere status, distinguishing Robinson; no opinion commanded a majority. Used for the act-versus-status boundary and for the point that Robinson is read narrowly.

sourceRecords.title: In re Winship, 397 U.S. 358 (1970)
sourceRecords.provider: Library of Congress (United States Reports, volume 397)
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion of the United States; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read the bound U.S. Reports scan directly. Verified: argued January 20, 1970, decided March 31, 1970; opinion by Justice Brennan; the Court 'explicitly hold[s] that the Due Process Clause protects the accused against conviction except upon proof beyond a reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime with which he is charged'; the case arose from a New York Family Court delinquency adjudication of a 12-year-old under a preponderance standard, and the Court extended the reasonable-doubt requirement to the adjudicatory stage of juvenile proceedings. sourceRecords.title: Morissette v. United States, 342 U.S. 246 (1952)
sourceRecords.provider: Library of Congress (United States Reports, volume 342)
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion of the United States; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read the bound U.S. Reports scan directly. Verified: argued October 9-10, 1951, decided January 7, 1952; criminal intent is an essential element of an offense under 18 U.S.C. 641, and 'mere omission ... of any mention of intent is not to be construed as eliminating that element from the crimes defined'; the opinion traces the rise of 'public welfare offenses'. Supports the presumption in favour of a mens rea requirement and the framing of strict liability as an exception.

sourceRecords.title: United States v. Bailey, 444 U.S. 394 (1980)
sourceRecords.provider: Library of Congress (United States Reports, volume 444)
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion of the United States; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read the bound U.S. Reports scan directly. Verified in the Court's mens rea discussion: the common-law dichotomy of 'general intent' and 'specific intent' is described as a source of confusion, quoting four incompatible usages from LaFave and Scott; the Model Penal Code approach replaces the elastic term 'intent' with a hierarchy commonly identified, in descending order of culpability, as purpose, knowledge, recklessness, and negligence (citing Model Penal Code section 2.02); the distinction between purpose and knowledge is often unimportant; culpability must be 'faced separately with respect to each material element of the crime'; 'Principles derived from common law as well as precepts suggested by the American Law Institute must bow to legislative mandates'; footnote 4 notes that strict liability crimes fall outside the hierarchy and that under the Model Penal Code the only strict liability offenses are 'violations' punishable by fine, forfeiture, or other civil penalty rather than imprisonment (section 2.05(1)(a)).

sourceRecords.title: Staples v. United States, 511 U.S. 600 (1994)
sourceRecords.provider: Library of Congress (United States Reports, volume 511)
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion of the United States; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read the bound U.S. Reports scan directly. Verified: argued November 30, 1993, decided May 23, 1994; to convict under 26 U.S.C. 5861(d) the government had to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant knew his rifle had the characteristics bringing it within the statutory definition of a machinegun; statutory silence on knowledge does not by itself dispense with mens rea; the public welfare offense line involves statutes regulating dangerous or deleterious devices, products, or obnoxious waste materials; the potentially harsh penalty of up to ten years' imprisonment confirmed the Court's reading, since the cases that defined the public welfare offense almost uniformly involved light penalties such as fines or short jail terms.

sourceRecords.title: Burrage v. United States, 571 U.S. 204 (2014)
sourceRecords.provider: Library of Congress (United States Reports, volume 571)
sourceRecords.license: Judicial opinion of the United States; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read the bound U.S. Reports scan directly. Verified: argued November 12, 2013, decided January 27, 2014; causation is 'a hybrid concept, consisting of two constituent parts: actual cause and legal cause', with legal cause 'often called the proximate cause' (citing LaFave and Model Penal Code section 2.03); 'results from' imposes a requirement of actual causality, ordinarily but-for causation; the Model Penal Code formulation that conduct causes a result if it is 'an antecedent but for which the result in question would not have occurred' (section 2.03(1)(a)) is 'the minimum requirement for a finding of causation'; a contributing act is still a but-for cause where the other factors alone would not have produced the result; the death-results enhancement is an element that must be submitted to the jury.

sourceRecords.title: Borden v. United States, No. 19-5410 (U.S. June 10, 2021) (plurality opinion)
sourceRecords.provider: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School
sourceRecords.notes: Read the opinion text on LII (argued November 3, 2020; decided June 10, 2021). Verified the plurality's statement of the four mental states 'in descending order of culpability: purpose, knowledge, recklessness, and negligence', with citations to Model Penal Code sections 2.02(2)(a), 2.02(2)(b)(ii), 2.02(2)(c) and 2.02(2)(d): purposefully means consciously desiring the result; knowingly means awareness that the result is practically certain; recklessly means consciously disregarding a substantial and unjustifiable risk in gross deviation from accepted standards; negligently means failing to perceive such a risk one should be aware of. The opinion itself is a government edict; the record is kept reference-only because the LII page carries its own site material, and no U.S. Reports page number was available on the page, so the docket-and-date citation form is used.

sourceRecords.title: California Penal Code section 20 - Union of act and intent
sourceRecords.license: State statute; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read live. The section, enacted in 1872 and still in force, provides that in every crime or public offense there must exist a union, or joint operation of act and intent, or criminal negligence. Used as a statutory illustration of the concurrence requirement in one state; not offered as the rule in any other jurisdiction.

sourceRecords.title: California Penal Code section 270 - Parent's failure to provide for a minor child
sourceRecords.license: State statute; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read live. A parent who wilfully omits, without lawful excuse, to furnish necessary clothing, food, shelter, medical attendance, or other remedial care for a minor child is guilty of a misdemeanor punishable by a fine not exceeding $2,000, imprisonment in the county jail not exceeding one year, or both, with greater exposure after a judicial paternity adjudication. Used as a verified example of a status-relationship duty codified by statute, so that an omission can satisfy the act element; state law varies.

sourceRecords.title: California Penal Code section 1096 - Presumption of innocence and reasonable doubt
sourceRecords.license: State statute; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read live (as amended by Stats. 1995, ch. 46). The defendant is presumed innocent; the effect of the presumption is to place on the state the burden of proving guilt beyond a reasonable doubt; reasonable doubt is defined as leaving jurors unable to say they feel an abiding conviction of the truth of the charge. Used to show how a state codifies the Winship standard.

sourceRecords.title: 26 U.S.C. 7203 - Willful failure to file return, supply information, or pay tax
sourceRecords.provider: Office of the Law Revision Counsel, U.S. House of Representatives
sourceRecords.license: United States Code; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Read live (text stated as in effect on August 17, 2026). A person required to pay tax or to make a return, keep records, or supply information who wilfully fails to do so at the time required is guilty of a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of not more than $25,000 ($100,000 for a corporation), imprisonment of not more than one year, or both, together with the costs of prosecution, with felony treatment for wilful violations of section 6050I. Used as a verified federal example of a statutory duty whose breach is an omission offence, and of a statute that states its own mental state ('wilfully').

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Criminal Law, 4.1: Criminal Elements
sourceRecords.license: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 (as stated on the page)
sourceRecords.notes: Verified live; the page states a CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 licence. Supports the standard teaching frame: every crime has at least a criminal act, a criminal intent, and concurrence, with causation and harm added for result crimes and attendant circumstances for some offences; the voluntariness requirement and the Model Penal Code section 2.01(2) list of movements that are not voluntary acts; that thoughts alone cannot be criminalized; and the categories of legal duty that make an omission criminal. Because the NonCommercial term is not clearly compatible with this project, no wording is reused; concepts only, and each case and statute cited here was checked against the primary source.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Criminal Law, 4.2: Criminal Intent
sourceRecords.license: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 (as stated on the page)
sourceRecords.notes: Verified live. Supports the course-standard presentation of the common-law intents (malice aforethought, specific intent, general intent) alongside the Model Penal Code's purposely, knowingly, recklessly and negligently; the distinction between motive and criminal intent; the concurrence requirement that act and intent exist at the same moment; and strict liability offences as an exception with no intent element, often in vehicle or tax codes. Concepts only; no wording reused.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Criminal Law, 4.3: Causation and Harm
sourceRecords.license: CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 (as stated on the page)
sourceRecords.notes: Verified live. Supports the two-step causation analysis taught in criminal law courses: but-for or factual cause, then legal or proximate cause tested by objective foreseeability, with the Model Penal Code section 2.03(2)(b) 'too remote or accidental' formulation, and intervening superseding causes that cut a defendant off from liability for the result. Concepts only; the but-for rule and the hybrid structure were independently confirmed against Burrage.
